summary: Animal camouflage for ages 5–7: many animals have colours and patterns that help them blend into their surroundings, either to hide FROM predators (prey) or to SNEAK UP on prey (predators). Teach the definition (blending in), then make the purpose felt by contrasting right vs wrong backgrounds, and include seasonal colour-change (e.g. Arctic hares in many areas, ptarmigan, and stoats in snowy regions are white in winter and brownish in summer; some far-northern Arctic hares stay white all year). Keep it observational: the animal HAS a feature that happens to match its home — it does not decide to paint itself. Hands-on manipulation (moving an animal between backgrounds, changing the season) makes the purpose concrete; search/spot activities provide the hook and a lighter check.
misconceptions: Thinking the animal consciously decides to change or 'paint' its colours to match — rather than being born with (or seasonally growing) patterns that fit its surroundings.
Believing camouflage is only for hiding from predators, missing that predators also use it to sneak up on prey.
Assuming camouflage makes an animal invisible everywhere, not realising it only works against the RIGHT background (and fails on the wrong one).
Treating an animal's colours/patterns as mere decoration rather than a feature with a survival job.
Confusing camouflage (blending in) with mimicry/warning colours (standing out to look dangerous) — keep to blending-in at this age.

activities.title: Spot the hidden animal
steps: Search a busy scene (a leafy branch, a seabed, tree bark) for an animal that is hard to find — e.g. a leaf insect among leaves, a flatfish on the seabed, a moth on bark.
Point to where you think the animal is hiding, then reveal its outline to check (outlining the hidden shape, or lifting a flap, makes a good reveal).
Say out loud why the fox or hawk would also find it hard to see.
activities.insight: The difficulty of finding the animal yourself is direct evidence that its colours and patterns match its surroundings — this is what 'blending in' means.

activities.title: Move the animal onto the wrong background
steps: Start with a camouflaged animal (e.g. a green leaf insect) on its matching background where it is hard to see.
Move the same animal onto a mismatched background (a grey rock or brown trunk) and notice how it now stands out.
Describe what might happen next: a predator would be much more likely to spot the exposed animal.
Try it in reverse: play the predator (e.g. a tiger whose stripes melt into tall grass) and see how blending helps the HUNTER creep up on prey.
activities.insight: Camouflage only works on the RIGHT background; on the wrong one the animal is much easier to see, so it is more likely to be caught. The same feature serves two jobs — hiding from predators AND sneaking up on prey.

activities.title: Change the season
steps: Watch a scene change from summer to winter (e.g. snow falls, moving a slider or stepping through the seasons).
Choose the Arctic hare's coat colour: leave it brown on the snow, then switch it to white.
Compare: brown on snow stands out glaringly; white on snow nearly disappears.
Say what the hare's coat does across the year and why brown would be a bad idea in winter snow.
activities.insight: Some animals change colour over time so they keep matching their surroundings as the seasons change — the match, not any one fixed colour, is what hides them.

activities.title: Same caterpillar, two backgrounds — predict and explain
steps: Look at two IDENTICAL green caterpillars: one on a green leaf, one on brown tree bark.
Before looking closely, predict which a hungry bird would find faster, and say WHY.
Explain which caterpillar is safer and connect it to whether the bird can spot it.
Answer a follow-up: would a white snow-hare be well hidden in green summer? Why not?
activities.insight: Because the two caterpillars are identical and only the background differs, safety comes from the colour MATCHING the surroundings — not from the colour by itself.

checkQuestion: Here are two caterpillars that are exactly the same green colour. One is sitting on a green leaf. The other is sitting on the brown bark of a tree trunk. A hungry bird is flying about looking for caterpillars to eat. Which caterpillar is safer — and why?
checkAnswer: The green caterpillar on the green leaf is safer, because its colour matches the leaf, so it blends in and the bird finds it hard to see. The identical green caterpillar on the brown trunk stands out against the brown and is easy for the bird to spot.
